title: The Structural AI Adoption Gap in Travel: Spending at Scale Before Returns Are Certain
summary: The travel industry is investing in intelligent solutions. Are you? Discover the risks, gaps, and strategies that shape structural AI adoption at scale.
body_markdown:
Structural AI adoption in the[travel industry](https://www.concentrix.com/industries/travel-transport-tourism/) is speeding up, but something’s missing. At first glance, the headline numbers from travel’s AI investment seem like a success story.[According to 2025 reports, more than 90% of organizations have already implemented AI tools.](https://www.pata.org/member-chapter-news-1/study-90-of-business-travel-managers-are-using-ai-but-opportunities-in-corporate-travel-abound) Agentic AI is finally moving from pilot to production.


Dig one layer deeper, and a more complicated picture emerges. According to the same source, 42% percent of organizations can’t calculate a clear return on their AI investments. Implementation hurdles are the top adoption barrier, cited ahead of talent and budget.


[And 52% of department-level AI initiatives globally are operating without formal approval or oversight](https://www.ey.com/en_gl/newsroom/2026/03/ey-survey-autonomous-ai-is-no-longer-theoretical-as-adoption-grows-despite-ongoing-trust-concerns) , a governance gap that grows more consequential as the decisions AI is making become more consequential.


This is the reality of AI in travel right now: broad adoption: genuine momentum, unresolved value capture, and asymmetric risk calculus that drives organizations to rush to invest without considering how it’ll impact infrastructure, data, and governance.


## The Risk Calculus Driving the Race


Most travel companies are investing because the cost of falling behind a competitor that figures it out first is existential, while the cost of investing too prematurely is, at worst, a recoverable capital allocation error. That asymmetry is what produces simultaneous heavy investment across major travel players at a moment when nearly half of the industry still can’t show ROI gains.


Each company faces the same calculation: the downside of investing in AI that doesn’t yet deliver is a recoverable profit and loss (P&L) line item.


The downside of a competitor that successfully achieves AI-driven personalization, dynamic pricing, or autonomous disruption management, at a level travelers trust and expect, is a structural loss of market position that can potentially compound over years.


It’s a rational response to a competitive environment where the timing of capability development matters more than short-term efficiency. The organizations that are likely to lose out on the gains from structural AI adoption and investment are those that interpret ROI ambiguity as a signal to wait rather than as a signal to invest with more precision.


## What’s Really Behind the Barriers to Adoption


The barriers to structural AI adoption in travel are organizational and data-derived, a distinction that changes where solutions need to come from.


Implementation complexity is the leading barrier, cited by[46% of travel managers. Lack of internal AI talent follows at 19%. Budget constraints, notably, trail at 14%,](https://www.pata.org/member-chapter-news-1/study-90-of-business-travel-managers-are-using-ai-but-opportunities-in-corporate-travel-abound) meaning capital is available for AI investment.


Execution is where the friction lives. There is another critical data layer:[42% of organizations report that they lack access to sufficient proprietary data to meaningfully customize AI models](https://www.ibm.com/think/insights/ai-adoption-challenges) , leaving them dependent on generic solutions that offer no competitive differentiation.


The common thread is that none of the four barriers can be resolved by getting a better model or signing a larger cloud contract. Structural AI adoption requires organizational transformation. This includes governance structures, data infrastructure, workforce capability, and change management. That’s a slower, harder problem than the technology itself.


## Differences in AI Trust by Generation


Layered onto the organizational challenges is a consumer-side complexity that resists simple resolution. AI adoption among travelers is not a single curve moving uniformly in one direction.


[40% of travelers under 35 already use AI tools in trip planning, compared to 20% of travelers over 55.](https://www.globalrescue.com/common/blog/detail/younger-travelers-lead-the-way-in-using-ai-for-trip-planning-older-travelers-remain-cautious/) The gap has direct implications for product design, channel strategy, and service delivery. Trust compounds the divide: just 4% of travelers say they’re comfortable acting on suggestions generated exclusively by AI, while 45% still favor human input.


A platform optimized for AI-native younger travelers will frustrate older high-value segments. A platform designed around traditional service expectations will feel inadequate to younger generations accustomed to AI-enabled travel planning.


Structural AI adoption comes down to trust.[Disruption management is the use case where AI agents have the highest potential ROI for travel companies.](https://www.concentrix.com/insights/blog/top-5-agentic-ai-use-cases-in-travel/) Deploying autonomous AI in that context, without first earning trust through lower-stakes interactions, creates failure scenarios that set adoption back to square one.


The practical implication for travel operators: trust for consequential decisions is earned incrementally through repeated positive experiences at lower stakes as opposed to a single high-capability product launch.


## The Agentic AI Adoption Threshold


The industry’s direction is unambiguous. AI in travel is moving from assistance to delegation.[In a Concentrix and Everest Group study of travel industry leaders, 56% said they are actively interested in deploying agentic AI for complex issue resolution through AI-augmented human support.](https://www.concentrix.com/insights/fact-sheet/ai-agents-for-travel/)


The organizations building infrastructure to deploy agentic AI responsibly are accruing an advantage that compounds. Disruption management, flight cancellations, rebooking, and proactive traveler communication, represents the highest-value near-term use case.


The ROI is measurable, the traveler benefit is immediate, and the operational complexity is manageable with the right human-AI collaboration architecture in place. The governance dimension requires equal investment.


In travel, where a single flawed AI decision can affect thousands of journeys simultaneously, that gap carries real operational and reputational exposure.


## The Rewards of Aligning Structural AI Adoption with Operational Realities


When travel businesses that[align AI investment with strategic priorities and operational realities](https://www.concentrix.com/insights/research/age-of-intelligent-transformation-scaling-ai/) , it will define what success looks like in the years ahead. Concentrix’s AI Readiness and Activation framework is built around this approach, embedding governance architecture into deployment from the outset. Some takeaways to consider:


- Treat AI investment as an operational capability that interfaces directly with core travel workflows, not as a standalone technology experiment.
- Invest in data infrastructure and governance so that AI systems can act on reliable, comprehensive datasets.
- Define measurable business outcomes before scaling AI, using those metrics to guide prioritization and resource allocation.
